paragraphs: The paper introduces a fast nearest-neighbor classifier built around a binary Correlation Matrix Memory, or CMM, neural network. The central engineering challenge is making classification data fit the memory's binary input requirements. The authors develop a robust encoding method to support this step, connecting the classifier's input representation to the machinery that performs the computation.

The work includes both software and hardware implementations. The dedicated CMM hardware is reported to run more than 200 times faster than a contemporary mid-range workstation and to scale to very large problems. That hardware comparison is distinct from the reported speed improvements for the complete classification method on benchmark tasks.

Against a simple k-nearest-neighbor method on several benchmarks, the CMM classifier has less than 1% lower accuracy while providing speedups exceeding four times in software and twelve times in hardware. These results describe an empirical accuracy–speed tradeoff: the new representation and implementation substantially accelerate classification while retaining accuracy close to the comparison method on the tested tasks.
neurips-1998-a-high-performance-k-nn-cla.tldr: A binary memory-based nearest-neighbor classifier achieves substantial benchmark speedups with less than 1% lower accuracy than a simple k-NN method.

paragraphs: Visual search involves locating a target among distracting items. A target with a distinctive feature can stand out immediately, while one identified by an absent feature or a combination of features can be harder to find. The paper addresses the mechanisms behind these differences in the ease of detecting a target.

A second puzzle is that exchanging the target and the background can change search difficulty. The same pair of visual patterns can therefore produce different search experiences depending on which pattern forms the background. Explaining this asymmetry requires accounting for the relationship between a target and its surroundings, alongside the properties of the target itself.

The paper shows that a model of segmentation in primary visual cortex, V1, based on interactions within the cortex can explain many qualitative aspects of visual search. Its contribution is to connect the separation of visual regions with both pop-out and search asymmetry. The stated result concerns qualitative patterns of behavior, supporting this cortical interaction model as an explanation for several observed search phenomena.
neurips-1998-a-v1-model-of-pop-out-and-a.tldr: A V1 segmentation model based on intracortical interactions explains many qualitative patterns of visual pop-out and search asymmetry.

paragraphs: The paper presents a procedure for choosing a wavelet basis when fitting a function to sampled data. The basis determines the collection of functions used to represent the fitted relationship. Selecting it is therefore part of deciding what kinds of shapes the regression model can express, rather than simply estimating coefficients within a fixed representation.

The method uses cross-validation to choose both the basis and a threshold. These two choices address the representation and the threshold applied in the regression procedure together. The selection process can also incorporate prior knowledge about smoothness or the shape of the basis functions, allowing expectations about the problem to influence which representations are considered appropriate.

The authors demonstrate the procedure on widely published sampled functions and contrast its results with other methods based on basis functions. The contribution is a data-guided selection process that also accommodates prior structural knowledge. The abstract establishes that the method is demonstrated and compared, without asserting that a particular basis or selection rule is uniformly best across regression problems.
neurips-1998-basis-selection-for-wavelet.tldr: The paper selects wavelet bases and thresholds through cross-validation while allowing prior knowledge about smoothness and basis shape.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression commonly relates outputs through a measure of distance between their inputs. In the formulation considered here, a positive definite matrix determines that distance. The usual diagonal choice weights input coordinates separately. The paper asks what becomes possible when the matrix can instead contain relationships between different coordinates and is tuned using training data.

An analysis of the matrix's eigenstructure shows that this more general distance effectively constructs hidden features. These features correspond to directions formed from combinations of the original input coordinates. The authors also explain that the data determine the dimensionality of the resulting hidden-feature space, linking the learned distance measure to the representation used for prediction.

On two test problems, predictions made with the general matrix outperform predictions using a diagonal matrix. This is evidence for the value of learning relationships among input directions in those examples. The broader methodological contribution is the interpretation: adjusting the covariance's distance measure can simultaneously learn useful features, making representation discovery part of Gaussian process regression.
neurips-1998-discovering-hidden-features.tldr: Learning a general distance matrix in Gaussian process regression discovers hidden features and improves predictions over a diagonal matrix on two test problems.

paragraphs: The paper develops two aspects of nonlinear latent variable models built with radial basis functions. These models provide a setting for representing data through latent variables, including low-dimensional representations intended for visualization. The work addresses both what kinds of representations the model should permit and how its likelihood can be evaluated using latent samples.

The first development considers priors or constraints on the allowable models as a way to preserve data structure in a low-dimensional view. A visualization is useful when its arrangement retains meaningful structure from the data. Restricting or favoring particular models provides a way to bring that objective into the construction of the representation.

The second development introduces a resampling approach that makes more effective use of latent samples during likelihood evaluation. It concerns the computation used to assess the model, complementing the first development's concern with representational structure. Together, the two contributions address the quality of the visual representation and the use of samples in evaluating the nonlinear latent variable model.
neurips-1998-exploratory-data-analysis-u.tldr: The paper develops structure-preserving model constraints and more effective likelihood resampling for radial basis function latent variable models.

paragraphs: Learning Real-Time A*, or LRTA*, alternates planning with taking actions. Although it had been shown to solve search problems efficiently in known environments, this paper examines reaching a specified goal in an initially unknown environment. Here, movement also serves exploration: an unvisited location remains a possible place to discover the goal.

The authors establish that uninformed LRTA* with maximal lookahead follows a shortest path to the nearest unvisited state. This gives a precise account of the exploration behavior induced by the algorithm under those conditions. Choosing the nearest unexplored possibility appears attractive because each immediate exploration decision minimizes the distance to a new state.

The paper nevertheless shows that this behavior does not minimize worst-case plan-execution time among uninformed exploration methods. Locally short trips to unexplored locations do not establish the strongest worst-case guarantee for the overall search. The result also matters to reinforcement learning because many methods share LRTA*'s combination of asynchronous dynamic programming, interleaved planning and action, and optimism about unknown possibilities.
neurips-1998-exploring-unknown-environme.tldr: Uninformed LRTA* with maximal lookahead explores the nearest unvisited state, but this strategy does not minimize worst-case execution time.

paragraphs: The paper studies inference in large Bayesian networks organized into layers and represented by directed acyclic graphs. The task is to determine marginal probabilities for variables of interest. Exact inference can be computationally intractable in these networks, creating a gap between specifying a probabilistic model and being able to use it for practical reasoning.

The proposed algorithms exploit averaging effects at nodes with many parents. Having many incoming influences supplies structure that the approximation can use. The algorithms produce rigorous lower and upper bounds on the desired probabilities, so their output brackets the answer instead of providing only an unqualified approximate value.

The authors prove that these bounds become exact in the large-network limit and provide rates describing convergence. This makes network size part of the theoretical explanation for the approximation's accuracy. The result supports effective inference in the studied large, layered networks despite the difficulty of exact computation, while distinguishing finite-network bounds from the exactness obtained in the stated limit.
neurips-1998-inference-in-multilayer-net.tldr: Averaging effects enable rigorous probability bounds for layered Bayesian networks that become exact in the large-network limit.

paragraphs: Learning a model of motion becomes harder when observations are noisy and the motion includes multiple classes of behavior. The abstract distinguishes this setting from simple, directly observed autoregressive processes. It also notes that expectation-maximization combined with Kalman filtering can handle approximate observations, but does not address the more complex multiple-class dynamics considered here.

The paper combines expectation-maximization with CONDENSATION, an algorithm that propagates sets of random samples. This substitutes a sample-based treatment of uncertain motion for the Kalman-filtering approach discussed in the abstract. The combination provides a way to learn dynamical models when uncertainty about the observations occurs alongside multiple classes of motion.

Experiments use visually observed juggling, and plausible dynamical models emerge from the learning process. The stated finding is that this combination can recover credible motion descriptions in that setting. Its significance lies in extending the learning approach to a richer kind of dynamics, where modeling uncertainty and distinguishing different motion classes are both part of the problem.
neurips-1998-learning-multi-class-dynami.tldr: Combining expectation-maximization with CONDENSATION learns plausible models of multiple motion classes from visually observed juggling.

paragraphs: The paper develops a speech recognition framework that models the geometry of acoustic trajectories. It considers a continuous variable tracing a smooth multidimensional curve together with a discrete variable representing a phonetic transcription. The key choice is to make the discrete process evolve according to distance traveled along the curve, measured by arc length.

Arc length depends on the curve's geometry rather than how quickly it is traversed. Consequently, the resulting Markov processes on curves produce transcription predictions that are invariant to nonlinear changes in timing. Within this formulation, traversing the same acoustic curve at a varying rate does not change the predicted relationship between the trajectory and the transcription.

The authors apply the framework to recognizing New Jersey town names and connected alpha-digits. On both tasks, these models achieve lower word error rates than comparably trained hidden Markov models. The experiments support the usefulness of the geometric approach on those tasks, while the model's timing invariance explains the particular representational property the method is designed to provide.
neurips-1998-markov-processes-on-curves-.tldr: Markov processes indexed by acoustic curve length provide timing-invariant predictions and outperform comparably trained hidden Markov models on two speech tasks.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning method using an actor–critic architecture. The actor supplies the action-selection component, while the critic provides an evaluation component. Both are represented by Normalized Gaussian Networks, which combine local linear regression units. This gives the two parts of the learning system a shared type of function approximation.

The networks are trained with an online expectation-maximization algorithm developed in the authors' earlier work. The combination brings that network-training procedure into reinforcement learning for control problems with continuous states and actions. The local regression units provide the representation through which the actor and critic learn their respective functions.

The authors test the method on swinging up and stabilizing a single pendulum and on balancing a double pendulum near its upright position. The experimental results show good control with a small number of trial-and-error attempts. These findings support the method's applicability to continuous optimal-control problems through the demonstrated pendulum tasks, without establishing that every such problem will require similarly few trials.
neurips-1998-reinforcement-learning-base.tldr: An actor–critic method trained through online EM achieves good continuous pendulum control with relatively few trial-and-error attempts.

paragraphs: The paper investigates reinforcement learning when an agent observes only part of its environment. It focuses on memoryless policies, which choose actions from the current observation. Earlier empirical work found that Sarsa with eligibility traces could efficiently find optimal policies within this restricted policy class on partially observable decision problems.

Eligibility traces provide short-term memory during learning by assigning delayed rewards to preceding observation–action pairs. This learning memory is distinct from the eventual policy's dependence on the current observation alone. The authors ask how much of the trace history is needed for the learning algorithm to retain its ability to find optimal memoryless policies.

They apply a k-step truncated variant of Sarsa with eligibility traces to four test problems. The experiments show that the traces can be substantially shortened without losing that ability on the evaluated problems. The finding suggests that long reward-credit histories were unnecessary in these cases, while remaining an empirical result about the tested problems and optimality within the memoryless policy class.
neurips-1998-the-effect-of-eligibility-t.tldr: On four partially observable test problems, substantially truncated eligibility traces still allow Sarsa to find optimal memoryless policies.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes the capacity of neural networks whose activation functions consist of polynomial pieces. It uses VC dimension, a measure of the variety of classification patterns a model family can realize. The goal is to characterize this capacity through architectural quantities rather than through experiments on a particular learning task.

The bounds depend on the number of adjustable parameters, network depth, number of hidden units, maximum number of polynomial segments, and maximum polynomial degree. The authors provide two upper bounds and a lower bound. Taken together, these results describe both limits on representational capacity and capacity that networks in the studied family can attain.

The bounds are tight in the stated cases of constant depth and depth proportional to the number of hidden units. For activations with a single polynomial segment, the abstract gives a tight order involving parameter count, depth, and the logarithm of polynomial degree. The contribution is therefore a quantitative connection between network structure and capacity, with matching characterizations in specified architectural regimes.
neurips-1998-tight-bounds-for-the-vc-dim.tldr: The paper bounds the VC dimension of piecewise-polynomial neural networks, obtaining tight characterizations in specified depth regimes.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how networks of simple neuron-like elements can represent complex relations and structures. This is a binding problem: a representation must capture how its elements belong together. The author starts from the observation that connectionist systems have historically struggled with representing and manipulating this kind of structured information.

The proposed direction uses time as part of a representation, alongside the arrangement of computing units. Synchronous firing had been suggested as a way to encode complex structures. The author identifies limitations of that approach and introduces an asynchronous binding model that extends it, broadening the temporal organization available for representing relationships.

The paper presents the asynchronous model as an effective representation of complex structures and argues that human cognitive architecture uses a similar mechanism. These are distinct claims: one concerns the proposed computational representation, while the other is an argument about cognition. The central contribution is the model's use of asynchronous temporal structure to address the representational challenge faced by simple interconnected units.
neurips-1998-utilizing-lime-asynchronous.tldr: An asynchronous binding model extends synchronous temporal representations to encode complex structures in connectionist systems.

paragraphs: Mixture models offer a statistical approach to clustering, and expectation-maximization is a common method for fitting them. The paper addresses a computational obstacle: EM repeatedly accesses the data, making its use expensive on enormous datasets. The proposed algorithm uses multiresolution kd-trees to reduce the cost of EM-based clustering.

The authors report a dramatic cost reduction, with savings increasing linearly with the number of data points. This claim concerns the growth of the savings; it should not be read as a claim that total runtime becomes independent of dataset size. The method is presented for maximum-likelihood estimation of Gaussian mixture models.

The abstract also identifies broader applications. Non-Gaussian models are covered when their class densities are monotonic in Mahalanobis distance. Other stated applications include clusters with mixed categorical and numerical data and Bayesian methods such as Autoclass. The contribution therefore combines an acceleration method for Gaussian mixture fitting with explicitly described routes to other clustering settings, including a condition on the non-Gaussian case.
neurips-1998-very-fast-em-based-mixture-.tldr: Multiresolution kd-trees substantially reduce EM clustering costs, with reported savings growing linearly with dataset size.

paragraphs: A neuronal population vector summarizes the coordinated activity of many movement-related neurons. It can roughly indicate movement direction or velocity, but its relationship to movement may change with arm posture. The paper investigates how the desired movement direction, actual movement direction, and population-vector direction relate within a model of cortical motor commands.

The model is a two-layer self-organizing neural network that combines broadly tuned muscular proprioceptive information with visual information in Cartesian coordinates. It produces angular motor commands for the initial movement of a two-link arm. Training uses motor babbling at five positions, linking the model's sensory inputs to its motor-command representation.

Simulations produce appropriate movement directions across much of the workspace. Near its extremes, small differences between desired and actual trajectories coincide with much larger deviations of the population vector from both. These results suggest that the population vector can misrepresent cortical processing even when the modeled movement remains relatively accurate, making it an imperfect summary of the computation generating a reach.
neurips-1998-where-does-the-population-v.tldr: A reaching model shows that large population-vector errors can accompany small movement errors, questioning the vector's fidelity as a summary of cortical processing.

paragraphs: Human reaction times vary across repetitions of a sensory–motor task. This study examines one possible contributor: variation in the response timing of neuronal populations at different stages of visual processing. It tests a view in which precise timing information becomes less well preserved as signals pass through successive processing stages.

The researchers apply blind source separation to MEG recordings from sensory–motor integration tasks. For each recovered visual source, they detect stimulus-related events on individual trials and estimate response latency and its variability. This makes the comparison about the timing of source responses across trials, including sources associated with both early and late visual processing.

In two participants completing four visual reaction-time tasks, the researchers reliably identify early and late visual sources. The standard deviation of response latency is smaller at early stages than at later ones. This supports the hypothesis that population response-time variability increases along visual processing stages in the studied setting, connecting a measured timing difference to the proposed loss of temporal precision.
neurips-1999-an-meg-study-of-response-la.tldr: MEG measurements in two participants support greater neuronal population response-time variability at later visual processing stages.

paragraphs: The paper studies separating multiple wideband sources recorded by an equal number of closely spaced receivers. It shows that separation can be feasible using second-order statistics when a physical model of signal mixing is incorporated. That physical description supplies structure to the problem of identifying which contributions belong to which source.

Under the considered model, parameter estimation can be reduced essentially to each signal's arrival direction and attenuation. The authors present two demixing methods, one operating in time and the other in frequency. Their experiments report successful demixing for signals arriving at different angles, supporting angular separation as a useful basis for the proposed methods.

The paper also addresses how to handle the separated outputs. Spatial information can resolve channel selection, and a Wiener filter applied afterward can reduce artifacts introduced by demixing. The overall approach connects a physical description of propagation with statistical separation and output refinement. Its feasibility claim is tied to the modeled mixing setting and the stated relationship between source and receiver counts.
neurips-1999-broadband-direction-of-arri.tldr: A physical mixing model enables broadband source separation through arrival directions, attenuations, and second-order statistics.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to build finite-memory predictors for sequences of symbols. It first maps fixed-length blocks from the training sequence into points inside a unit hypercube. Blocks sharing a longer suffix receive nearby representations, turning a relationship between recent symbolic histories into a relationship between spatial locations.

This construction expresses a Markov assumption: histories with long matching endings are likely to have similar continuations. The method then treats selecting prediction contexts as a resource-allocation problem. Vector quantization of the spatial representation determines those contexts, providing an automatic route from the sequence's block structure to a predictive model.

The authors compare their models with classical Markov models and variable-memory-length Markov models on three datasets with different memory and stochastic components. Their models perform better in those comparisons, and their construction is fully automatic. The latter is a particular contribution because the abstract identifies automatic construction as problematic for the variable-memory approach. The results support the combination of suffix-based geometry and context allocation on the tested datasets.
neurips-1999-building-predictive-models-.tldr: A spatial encoding of symbolic histories enables automatic predictive models that outperform classical and variable-memory Markov models on three datasets.

paragraphs: Belief propagation computes probabilistic information through local updates in a graph. Its correctness is established for singly connected models, while its empirical success on graphs containing loops raises harder theoretical questions. This paper analyzes arbitrary graph structures when the variables are jointly Gaussian, providing an analytical relationship between true posteriors and the results of loopy propagation.

The authors give sufficient conditions for convergence and prove that, whenever the algorithm converges in this Gaussian setting, its posterior means are correct. The qualification matters: arbitrary topology does not itself guarantee convergence, and correctness of the means is more specific than correctness of the entire posterior distribution.

The paper also studies max-product propagation beyond Gaussian distributions. Its convergence points in loopy networks maximize posterior probability over a particular large local neighborhood. This is a local optimality result rather than a guarantee of the global maximum. Together, the results explain specific forms of correctness that can survive loops and provide theoretical motivation for using propagation algorithms in a broader range of networks.
neurips-1999-correctness-of-belief-propa.tldr: For jointly Gaussian graphical models of any topology, belief propagation gives exact posterior means if it converges.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis applied to natural images can produce linear filters resembling properties of simple cells in primary visual cortex. This paper extends that approach to account for additional properties, especially the invariances associated with complex cells and the organization of components into a topography. Both extensions build on statistical relationships in natural images.

The first extension replaces independent scalar components with independent subspaces. In this model, the learned features exhibit phase and shift invariance, resembling complex-cell properties. The representational change is therefore from independence among individual components to independence among groups, allowing the model to capture a different kind of visual feature.

The second extension defines proximity between components through their higher-order correlations. Components that are strongly statistically dependent lie close together in the resulting topography. This produces both an organized arrangement and invariances resembling complex-cell behavior. The findings connect these properties to extensions of the image-statistics model, offering a computational account of their joint emergence without claiming that the model establishes the biological mechanism.
neurips-1999-emergence-of-topography-and.tldr: Extensions of ICA learn complex-cell-like invariances and component topography from natural-image statistics.

paragraphs: The paper develops nonlinear methods for extracting invariant features and distinguishing classes while incorporating prior knowledge. Invariance concerns retaining the relevant representation despite variations that the model is intended to disregard. Including prior knowledge makes the intended structure part of the learning method, connecting feature construction with the requirements of the discrimination task.

The authors use a common mathematical framework built around a nonlinear version of the Rayleigh coefficient. Within that framework, they propose nonlinear generalizations of Fisher's discriminant and oriented principal component analysis. Support Vector kernel functions provide the mechanism for expressing these nonlinear methods, bringing the two constructions into a shared kernel-based formulation.

Extensive simulations demonstrate the utility of the approach. The stated contribution combines prior knowledge, nonlinear feature extraction, and discrimination within one framework, rather than treating them as unrelated procedures. The evidence supports the usefulness of the proposed constructions in the simulations described, while the abstract does not assert a universal performance advantage or specify a particular kind of invariance for every application.
neurips-1999-invariant-feature-extractio.tldr: A unified kernel framework incorporates prior knowledge into nonlinear versions of Fisher's discriminant and oriented PCA for invariant learning.

paragraphs: Decoding a neural population requires inferring information from its joint activity, often without knowing the brain's true encoding process. The paper studies maximum-likelihood decoding with an inaccurate or deliberately simplified model. Its chosen simplification ignores pairwise correlations between neurons, reducing the statistical dependencies that the decoder must represent.

The authors prove asymptotic efficiency when neuronal correlations are uniform or limited in range. This is a conditional result about the specified correlation structures and an asymptotic regime. It shows that ignoring correlations can still preserve a strong statistical property under those conditions, despite the mismatch between the decoding model and the encoding process.

The work compares this decoder with maximum-likelihood inference using a faithful model and with center-of-mass decoding. The reported outcome is markedly reduced computational complexity alongside high decoding accuracy. The authors also discuss how correlation affects accuracy. Together, these results explain why a simplified population model can be useful: some representational inaccuracies can coexist with effective inference under the conditions studied.
neurips-1999-population-decoding-based-o.tldr: A decoder that ignores pairwise neural correlations can remain asymptotically efficient under specified correlation structures while reducing computational complexity.

paragraphs: The paper uses statistical physics to investigate regular and irregular Gallager-type error-correcting codes. Codewords are built from products of message bits selected through two randomly constructed sparse matrices. The numbers of nonzero entries in the matrices' rows and columns define a family of codes whose performance can be compared within this framework.

The analysis shows that many regular codes may reach Shannon's channel capacity in equilibrium. Other regular codes have slightly lower performance but may be more practically relevant. This distinction separates the equilibrium performance available to a code from the considerations that determine whether it is useful in practice.

To examine decoding, the authors use the TAP approach, which they identify with the commonly used belief-propagation decoder. They show that irregular codes may also reach capacity while having improved dynamical properties. The significance is the connection between code structure, equilibrium limits, and decoding dynamics: capacity-level potential and favorable decoding behavior are both addressed, with the capacity statements retaining their qualified form.
neurips-1999-regular-and-irregular-galla.tldr: Statistical-physics analysis finds that irregular Gallager-type codes may reach Shannon capacity with improved decoding dynamics.

paragraphs: In partially observable decision problems, an agent can represent uncertainty through a belief state: a probability distribution over underlying states. Reinforcement learning with this representation is promising for small problems. For larger ones, computing or storing the complete distribution can become intractable, making the representation itself a central obstacle to learning useful policies.

The paper investigates two reinforcement learning methods using full belief states and a new method using factored approximate belief states. The approximate approach builds on work showing that useful belief estimates can often be maintained while leaving out correlations between state variables. Factoring the belief representation addresses the burden of representing their full joint uncertainty.

The authors compare these methods on several established problems and report results demonstrating the importance of approximate belief representations for large problems. The contribution is to study approximation as part of the learning system, where its value depends on supporting policy learning as well as representing uncertainty. The stated findings support this direction without claiming that removing correlations preserves all information relevant to every decision problem.
neurips-1999-reinforcement-learning-usin.tldr: A new reinforcement learning method uses factored approximate beliefs to address the difficulty of full belief-state representations in large partially observable problems.

paragraphs: The paper addresses capacity control for models expressed as expansions in basis functions. Capacity control concerns restricting the richness of a fitted model, and uniform convergence bounds provide a way to analyze that restriction across a model family. The abstract notes that effective entropy-number-based bounds had largely been available in the support vector machine setting.

The authors extend these methods to expansions using arbitrary parameterized basis functions and to a broad range of regularization approaches. The scope covers general linear additive models. This broadens the class of function expansions for which the capacity-control analysis can be applied, connecting the theoretical treatment to more choices of basis and regularizer.

The extension relies on a data-dependent analysis of the eigenvalues of the corresponding design matrix. These eigenvalues provide information about the model's basis representation on the observed data. The contribution is thus a framework for deriving capacity-control bounds from that representation, with the data participating in the analysis rather than the result being tied solely to the support vector machine formulation.
neurips-1999-the-entropy-regularization-.tldr: A data-dependent eigenvalue analysis extends entropy-based capacity-control bounds to general linear additive models and diverse regularizers.
